opus-5.5.text:
Sure. So the traditional way people have thought about differential privacy, going back to the early work by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues, is what you might call the query-answering model. There's a trusted curator who holds a sensitive database, let's say medical records, and analysts come along and ask aggregate questions. How many patients over sixty have diabetes? What's the average cholesterol level in some subgroup? The curator answers each question, but adds carefully calibrated noise so that no single person's presence or absence in the data changes the answer distribution very much.

That works, but it has some real practical problems. Every question you answer uses up some of your privacy budget, so you have to be very careful about how many questions you allow and in what order. You need infrastructure that sits between the analysts and the data and manages that accounting. And analysts don't like it. They're used to having a data set in hand that they can poke at, run their favorite software on, and explore in ways they didn't plan in advance.

Synthetic data flips that around. Instead of answering questions one at a time, you use your privacy budget once, up front, to generate a whole new fake data set. It has the same schema, the same kinds of rows, but no row corresponds to a real person. The goal is that it preserves the statistical properties of the original data, at least for some large class of queries you care about, like all the low-order marginals or correlations between pairs or triples of attributes.

The nice thing is that differential privacy is closed under post-processing. Once you've generated that synthetic data set in a differentially private way, you can hand it to anybody and they can do whatever they want with it, ask as many questions as they like, train models on it, and they can't degrade the privacy guarantee. There's no ongoing budget to manage.

One way I like to think about the algorithms is as a game between two players. One player is trying to build a synthetic data set, and the other is an adversary, a query player, who looks for the question where the synthetic data and the real data disagree the most. The data player then fixes that discrepancy, the adversary finds the next worst query, and so on. Using no-regret learning dynamics, you can show this converges to a synthetic data set that's accurate on the whole class of queries simultaneously, and only the step where you consult the real data needs to be privatized.

The caveat, and I always try to be honest about this, is that there's no free lunch. Synthetic data will only be accurate for the kinds of statistics you designed it to preserve. If someone later asks about some subtle high-order interaction you didn't target, the answer could be quite wrong. And there are worst-case computational hardness results for doing this for very rich query classes. But in practice, with modern optimization heuristics, we and others have gotten these methods to work surprisingly well on real data sets, and I think it's one of the most promising ways to get differential privacy actually adopted, because it gives people the thing they want, which is data.

r001.rationale: It contrasts answering aggregate questions one at a time with noise against generating and releasing a new synthetic dataset.

r002.rationale: It says the synthetic dataset aims to preserve the original data’s statistical properties for a class of queries, such as low-order marginals and attribute correlations.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I usually set this up is to start with what I'd call the "query answering" model of differential privacy, which is the one most people encounter first. You have some sensitive dataset, say medical records, and an analyst comes along and asks a question: what fraction of patients over sixty have diabetes? The differentially private approach is to compute the true answer and then add a carefully calibrated amount of noise before releasing it, so that no individual's record has much influence on what gets published. And you can keep doing that, question after question, but every answer spends a little of your privacy budget, and eventually you run out. That's the fundamental tension: the more questions you answer, the more you leak, and the noise has to go up to compensate.

Synthetic data generation flips the interaction around. Instead of the data holder sitting there answering queries one at a time, you spend your privacy budget once, up front, to produce a brand new dataset. That dataset consists of fake records, fake people, who never existed, but it's constructed so that it preserves, approximately, the statistical structure of the real data. Correlations, marginals, the kinds of aggregate properties an analyst would care about. And then you just hand that synthetic dataset over. The analyst can run any query they want on it, as many times as they want, fit models to it, make plots, and none of that costs anything further in privacy terms, because the differential privacy guarantee was already paid for at the moment the synthetic data was released. Post-processing is free under differential privacy, and this is just post-processing.

Now, there's no free lunch here, and I think it's important to be honest about that. The synthetic data is only going to be accurate for the statistics you targeted when you generated it, or things closely related to them. If you built it to preserve all the two-way and three-way correlations among attributes and somebody comes along with a very exotic query that depends on some high-order interaction you didn't model, the answer they get off the synthetic data may be garbage, and the problem is they may not know it's garbage. Whereas in the interactive query model, the noise is explicit and you can reason about it. So there's a real tradeoff between the convenience and the sort of unlimited reuse of synthetic data versus the precision and the auditability of answering specific questions.

The reason I find synthetic data compelling anyway, and why a lot of our work at Penn has gone in this direction, is partly sociological rather than technical. Data scientists don't want to interact with a privacy oracle. They want a CSV file they can load into Python and explore. If you give people a dataset that looks and feels like real data, they'll actually use it, and the privacy protection comes along for the ride without them having to think about it. It also helps with the problem that in the interactive model you have to decide in advance who gets to ask questions and how to divide the budget among them, which is a governance nightmare. With synthetic data you release it once and the question of who gets access becomes a lot less fraught, because the release itself is already safe.

And I'd add that the machinery for generating this stuff has gotten quite good. The early approaches were essentially these game-theoretic constructions, where you think of it as a zero-sum game between a data generator trying to match the real distribution and an adversary trying to find a query where the synthetic data is wrong, and you iterate. More recently people have combined that with modern generative models and gradient-based methods, and the fidelity you can get at reasonable privacy levels, on realistic tabular data, is genuinely useful now. It's not a research curiosity anymore.

r001.rationale: It contrasts adding calibrated noise to individual query answers with generating and releasing a new dataset of fake records.

r002.rationale: It says the synthetic dataset approximately preserves the real data’s statistical structure, including correlations and marginals.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to change what you release. Instead of keeping the private data behind an interface where someone asks a question and you return a noisy answer, you use the private data to generate a new, artificial data set. It has the same kinds of fields, and you want it to preserve statistical properties of the original population, but the rows aren’t simply copies of real people’s records.

Now, just calling data synthetic doesn’t make it private. The generation procedure itself needs to satisfy differential privacy. Roughly speaking, whether any one person’s record is included in the original data should make very little difference to the distribution of the synthetic data you release.

The attraction is that once you’ve released that differentially private data set, people can analyze it repeatedly without further spending the privacy budget. They can use their familiar tools, compute statistics, build models. Those are all computations on something you’ve already released privately.

The challenge is utility. You generally can’t promise that every possible analysis on the synthetic data will give the same answer as it would on the original data. So you need to decide which statistical properties or classes of questions you want to preserve, and how accurately. You’re trading the flexibility of having a data set people can work with against the difficulty of preserving the information they actually need.

r001.rationale: It contrasts releasing a newly generated artificial dataset with answering questions through an interface that returns noisy answers.

r002.rationale: It says the synthetic dataset is intended to preserve the original population’s statistical properties, and explains that selected properties can be preserved to some chosen accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about differential privacy is that you have a private database, and people ask aggregate questions about it. You compute an answer, add a carefully calibrated amount of noise, and release that noisy answer. But every time you do that, you use up some of your privacy budget, so you have to manage the collection of questions you’re answering.

Synthetic data takes a different approach. Instead of releasing answers to individual questions, you use a differentially private algorithm to generate an artificial dataset. The goal is for that artificial dataset to reproduce the statistical properties of the original data that you care about, while protecting the individuals whose records were used to create it.

Then you can give people the synthetic dataset, and they can analyze it without coming back to the private database. Those subsequent analyses don’t incur an additional privacy cost. The important caveat is that you’re not promising that the synthetic data will accurately answer every conceivable question. You need to specify what kinds of statistical relationships you want to preserve, and there’s a tradeoff between how accurately you preserve them and how much privacy you provide.

r001.rationale: It contrasts releasing a differentially private artificial dataset with answering individual aggregate questions by releasing noisy answers.

r002.rationale: It says the synthetic dataset aims to reproduce the original data’s statistical properties of interest.
